think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 6-year-old boy in an endemic setting presented with subacute fever, headache, and new-onset flowing choreiform limb movements initially diagnosed as Sydenham chorea and subsequently misdiagnosed as autoimmune encephalitis. The presentation created diagnostic tension between post-streptococcal movement disorders, autoimmune receptor encephalitides, and an occult basilar infectious meningoencephalitis with secondary basal ganglia vasculopathy.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint occurs following emergency triage and neurological physical examination characterizing the movement disorder, baseline complete blood count, serum electrolytes (identifying hyponatremia), normal chest radiography, and anti-streptolysin O (ASO) serology, immediately prior to diagnostic lumbar puncture, cerebrospinal fluid cytochemical/molecular analysis, and cranial computed tomography.
3. Differential Distinctions: Acute rheumatic fever / Sydenham chorea was suspected based on acute-to-subacute pediatric chorea, prompting empiric penicillin; however, major Jones criteria (carditis, arthritis, erythema marginatum) were absent and ASO titer was normal (<200 IU/mL). Autoimmune encephalitis was considered following therapy failure, leading to empiric valproic acid, but was refuted by the absence of psychiatric/behavioral changes, normal sensorium, negative anti-NMDA receptor antibodies, and profoundly hypoglycorrhachic CSF. Tuberculous meningitis presenting with chorea was established by close household contact history, marked lymphocytic pleocytosis, severe hyperproteinorrachia, undetectable CSF glucose, and CT confirmation of basal exudates, communicating hydrocephalus, and caudate/capsular arteritic infarcts.
case_prompt:
A 6-year-old, developmentally at par, right-handed Filipino male presented to our institution for evaluation of involuntary limb movements. Three weeks prior to presentation, he developed generalized headaches and intermittent, undocumented fevers, which subsequently became associated with involuntary dance-like flowing movements involving all four extremities. He was initially evaluated at an outside hospital, where he was diagnosed with acute rheumatic fever and received a course of parenteral penicillin. His diagnosis was subsequently revised to autoimmune encephalitis, and he was discharged on oral valproic acid syrup. Over the intervening days, his parents noted resolution of involuntary movements on the left side but persistent abnormal movements on the right, prompting consultation at our hospital.

Review of systems revealed no recurrent pharyngitis, cough, shortness of breath, gastrointestinal symptoms, easy fatigability, or arthralgias. The parents reported no alteration in sensorium, cognitive decline, behavioral changes, seizures, or focal weakness. The child had a history of close household contact exposure to an adult family member with chronic active pulmonary infectious disease, but had no personal chronic medical conditions, no prior viral exanthems, and no family history of movement disorders.

On physical examination, the child was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. He was alert, fully oriented, and interactive. General examination revealed no dysmorphic features, alopecia, Kayser-Fleischer rings, anterior cervical masses, or cutaneous lesions. Neurological examination demonstrated brief, non-rhythmic, non-stereotyped, flowing choreiform movements predominantly affecting the right lower extremity more than the right upper extremity, with minimal choreiform movements in the left upper extremity. Hand spooning and parakinesia were observed in the right upper extremity; no other involuntary movements or abnormal posturing were noted. Visual pursuit and saccades were intact. Muscle bulk and tone were normal, with 5/5 motor strength throughout. Reflexes were symmetric, with no upper motor neuron signs, nystagmus, dysmetria, or sensory deficits.

Initial triage laboratory evaluation revealed leukocytosis with a peripheral white blood cell count of 14.6 x 10^9/L (reference range: 4.5–11.0 x 10^9/L) and a hemoglobin of 113 g/L (reference range: 135–180 g/L). Serum biochemistry demonstrated hyponatremia with a sodium of 129 mmol/L (reference range: 135–145 mmol/L) and a random blood glucose of 82 mg/dL. Platelet count, serum creatinine, transaminases, calcium, and magnesium were all within normal limits. An emergency plain chest radiograph was normal. Anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titer was non-elevated at <200 IU/mL. Reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction for COVID-19 was negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Acute-to-subacute chorea following febrile illness in a school-aged child prompted an initial diagnosis of rheumatic chorea and empiric parenteral penicillin; however, other major Jones criteria (carditis, polyarthritis, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules) were absent and the anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titer was normal (<200 IU/mL).
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: He was initially managed at a different hospital as a case of rheumatic fever and was given a course of parenteral penicillin... Chest X-ray revealed normal findings and anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titer was <200 IU/mL (Normal: <200).

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered at the outside hospital after penicillin failed to resolve the chorea, leading to administration of valproic acid; ruled out by normal mental status, absence of psychiatric disturbances or seizures, negative anti-NMDA receptor antibodies, and profound CSF hypoglycorrhachia incompatible with uncomplicated autoimmune encephalitis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The diagnosis was subsequently revised to autoimmune encephalitis and he was later on discharged on oral valproic acid syrup... CSF gram stain and culture, acid-fast bacilli (AFB), Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR, and anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDA-r) antibody all came back negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: In a child residing in an endemic region with close household contact and subacute fever, lumbar puncture demonstrated profound hypoglycorrhachia (undetectable CSF glucose with blood glucose 82 mg/dL), marked hyperproteinorrachia (351 mg/dL), and lymphocytic pleocytosis (144 WBCs/mcL, 99% lymphocytes); despite negative acid-fast bacilli smear and PCR, tuberculous meningitis (BMRC Stage III) was clinically confirmed and supported on day 3 by contrast CT showing basal exudates, communicating hydrocephalus, and ischemic arteritic infarcts of the right caudate and internal capsule. Combination therapy with fixed-dose anti-TB medications and high-dose dexamethasone achieved prompt cessation of chorea.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Because of the subacute history of fever and headache plus the absence of apparent acquired causes of chorea, a lumbar puncture was performed to investigate for central nervous system (CNS) infections. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies demonstrated lymphocytic-predominant leukocytosis (WBC 144 x 106/L, Lymphocytes 99%), hyperproteinorrachia (351mg/dL; Normal: 12-60), and hypoglycorrhachia (undetectable; Normal: 40-70mg/dL). CSF gram stain and culture, acid-fast bacilli (AFB), Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR, and anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDA-r) antibody all came back negative. Given the endemicity of TB in the Philippines, the patient's known exposure to a confirmed case of TB, his subacute presentation, and the constellation of CSF findings, a diagnosis of Tuberculous Meningitis (TBM) British Medical Research Council (BMRC) Stage III was made and he was started on isoniazid/rifampicin/pyrazinamide/ethambutol 150/75/400/275 mg fixed-combination tablet, 2 tablets once a day and intravenous dexamethasone at 20 mg/day.

editor_comments: Distillation successfully executed according to Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology. Admission prompt focuses strictly on the initial clinical presentation, physical exam characterization of the chorea, baseline hematology, hyponatremia, and negative ASO titer, while excluding lumbar puncture, neuroimaging, pathogen names, and clinical course. Reasoning includes exact verbatim quotes.
